subtopics.name: Electric Force Between Two Point Charges

parts.problem_md:
Two charged objects X and Y are made to circle a point O. X and Y are at a distance, *d* = 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m and they have equal masses, where *m* = 1.7 × 10<sup>−9</sup> kg as shown in Fig. 1.1.

The objects carry an equal but opposite charge, where the magnitude *q* = 3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C.

![dae17afb-852e-4b5a-8723-1796e5ba2bd7-1](assets/001-dae17afb-852e-4b5a-8723-1796e5ba2bd7-1.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the acceleration of X and Y.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Distance, *d* = 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m
- Mass*, m* = 1.7 × 10<sup>−9</sup> kg
- Charge, *q* = 3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C
- Gravitational constant, *G* = 6.67 × 10<sup>−11</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>−2</sup>
- Permittivity of free space, *ε*<sub>*o*</sub> = 8.85 × 10<sup>−12</sup> C<sup>2</sup> N<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−2</sup>

Deduce an expression for the resultant force:

- X and Y are in a circular motion around O
- The forces which hold the particle in motion are gravity and the Coulomb force
- Resultant centripetal force, $F_{R}=F_{g}+F_{c}$

  - Where *F*<sub>*R*</sub> = resultant force, *F*<sub>*g*</sub> = force due to gravity, *F*<sub>*c*</sub> = Coulomb force

Find *F*<sub>*g*</sub>, the force due to gravity:

- $F_{g}=G\frac{Mm}{r^{2}}$
- Therefore $F_{g}=(6.67\times10^{-11})\times\frac{(1.7\times10^{-9})^{2}}{(1.8\times10^{-8})^{2}}=5.950\times10^{-13}N$ **[1 mark]**

Find *F*<sub>*c*</sub>, the Coulomb force by combining the equations for Coulomb's law and Coulomb's constant:

- $F_{c}=\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- Therefore $F_{c}=\frac{(3.2\times10^{-19})^{2}}{4π\times(8.85\times10^{-12})\times(1.8\times10^{-8})^{2}}=2.842\times10^{-12}N$ **[1 mark]**

Add the forces to find the resultant and use *F = ma* to find acceleration:

- $F_{R}=ma$
- Therefore, $a=\frac{(F_{g}+F_{c})}{m}$
- Therefore $a=\frac{(5.950\times10^{-13})+(2.842\times10^{-12})}{(1.7\times10^{-9})}=2.022\times10^{-3}$
- *a* = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m s<sup>−2</sup> (2 s.f.); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In many situations gravity can be taken as negligible, however in this situation the particles are close enough together that gravity plays a part.*

> *An alternative method to find the time period would use the equation  *$F_{R}=mω^{2}r$*, which introduces one extra step but still ends at the same place and same answer.*

> *Once the force has been found, acceleration can be obtained from circular motion equations.*

> *Finally, the last equation can be found two ways, either by deriving as suggested in the solution above, or, using quick dimensional analysis as a reminder. Notice that angular velocity is measured in 'per seconds', therefore time period must be, in effect, 'per angular velocity'.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Two charged objects X and Y are made to circle a point O. X and Y are at a distance, d = 1.8 × 10^−8 m and they have equal masses, where m = 1.7 × 10^−9 kg as shown in Fig. 1.1. The objects carry an equal but opposite charge, where the magnitude q = 3.2 × 10^−19 C. Calculate the acceleration of X and Y.
a = 2.0 × 10^−3 m s^−2 (2 s.f.)

Calculate the time required for the particles in part a) to make one complete orbit.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Acceleration of particles, *a *= 2.022 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m s<sup>−2</sup>
- Separation of particles, *d *= 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m

Recall the equation for centripetal acceleration and determine the angular velocity of X and Y:

- $a=ω^{2}r$
- $ω=\sqrt{\frac{a}{r}}$

- $ω=\sqrt{\frac{2.022\times10^{-3}}{0.5\times(1.8\times10^{-8})}}=473.99s^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Recall that for motion in a circle:

- $T=\frac{2π}{ω}$
- $T=\frac{2π}{473.99}=1.33\times10^{-2}s$ = 13 ms (2 s.f) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Two charged objects X and Y are made to circle a point O. X and Y are at a distance, d = 1.8 × 10^−8 m and they have equal masses, where m = 1.7 × 10^−9 kg as shown in Fig. 1.1. The objects carry an equal but opposite charge, where the magnitude q = 3.2 × 10^−19 C.

A torque is experienced by particles X and Y from part a) when placed in an electric field of strength 6.5 V m<sup>−1</sup>. The electric field acts perpendicular to the line between X and Y.

Calculate the magnitude and explain the presence of the instantaneous torque when the particles are just starting to move in the electric field.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Magnitude of each charge, *q *= 3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C
- Separation distance between charges, *d *= 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m
- Electric field strength, *E *= 6.5 V m<sup>−1 </sup>

Calculate the electric force on each charge, *F*:

- Recall: *F* = *qE *
- *F *= (3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup>) × 6.5
- *F *= 2.08 × 10<sup>−18</sup> N **[1 mark]**

Calculate the torque, *τ*:

- *τ *= *Fd*
- *τ *= (2.08 × 10<sup>−18</sup>) × (1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup>)
- *τ *= 3.744 × 10<sup>−26</sup> N m **[1 mark]**

Explain the presence of the torque:

- The electric force *F * produces a turning effect about the centre of the circle O; **[1 mark]**
- Without the electric field there is no torque present on X and Y to produce a turning effect; **[1 mark]**
- The force *F*  is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction on X and Y and acts perpendicular to the distance between them; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Look back through all your workings in previous parts of this question to obtain the variables you need for this part.*

parts.problem_md:

The particles X and Y in part a) are replaced with a gold nucleus `Au presubscript 79 presuperscript 197` of radius 7.0 fm, and an alpha particle of radius 1.7 fm. They are circling point O with the same separation *d *and are no longer in an electric field.

Show that the separation of the gold nucleus and the alpha particle is around 9 × 10<sup>−15</sup> larger than the separation of particles X and Y.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Radius of gold nucleus, *r*<sub>*g*</sub> = 7.0 fm = 7.0 × 10<sup>−15</sup> m
- Radius of alpha particle, *r*<sub>*α*</sub> = 1.7 fm = 1.7 × 10<sup>−15</sup> m
- Separation of particles, *d *= 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m

Determine the order of magnitude of the additional separation, Δ*r* caused by the gold and helium nuclei radii:

- Δ*r *= *r*<sub>*g*</sub>* *+ *r*<sub>*α *</sub>**[1 mark]**
- Δ*r *= (7.0 × 10<sup>−15</sup>) + (1.7 × 10<sup>−15</sup>) = 8.7 × 10<sup>−15</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows two point charges of + 6.0 nC and + 10.0 nC which are 67 mm apart.

Calculate the magnitude of the force exerted on the +10.0 nC charge by the +6.0 nC charge.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Separation between the two charges, *r* = 67 mm = 67 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- $Q_{1}$= +10.0 nC
- $Q_{2}$= +6.0 nC

From the formulae page:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>** OR **$\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$** **= 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the force:

- Coulomb’s Law: *F* = $\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- *F* = $\frac{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) \times ( 10.0 \times 10^{-9} } ) \times ( 6.0 \times 10^{- 9} )}{( 67 \times 10^{- 3} )^{2}}$**[1 mark]**
- *F* = 1.2 × 10<sup>–4</sup> N **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

> *Remember that the charges must be in Coulombs and the separation **r**  must be in metres for Coulomb's law**. *

> *The magnitude of this force is identical to the magnitude of the force exerted on the +6.0 nC charge by the +10.0 nC charge. The only thing that would change, is its direction (they would be in opposite directions).*

![img-a9a31a8e6fec-1](assets/004-img-a9a31a8e6fec-1.jpeg)

> *This is because the electric force is due to the interaction of **both** charges, not a force produced by just one, which is a common misconception.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows two point charges of + 6.0 nC and + 10.0 nC which are 67 mm apart.

State and explain what happens to the electric force on the 10.0 nC if the distance between the charges is doubled.
parts.solution_md:
The electric force on the 10.0 nC charge:

- Decreases by 4 / quarters; **[1 mark]**
- Because $F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$ / the force is inversely proportional to the separation between the charges <u>squared</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *We can see this if we put the numbers into the equation.*

> *If we say *$F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$* and **r**  becomes 2**r**  (the separation doubles), then the force becomes *$F = \frac{Q_{1} Q_{2} }{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} ( 2 r )^{2}} = F = \frac{Q_{1} Q_{2} }{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} 4 r^{2}}$*.*

> *This new force is now **four times smaller** than the original.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

An alpha particle and an aluminium nucleus are isolated in a vacuum, as shown in Fig. 1.1. Each nucleus may be considered to be a point mass with a point charge.

State **one **similarity and **one **difference between the gravitational force field and the electric force field around the nuclei.
parts.solution_md:
A similarity between the force fields is:

- (Electric and gravitational) <u>forces</u> both follow an inverse square law with distance / $F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$; **[1 mark] ** **OR**
- (Electric and gravitational) <u>potentials</u> both follow an inversely proportional relationship with distance /** **$V\propto\frac{1}{r}$; **[1 mark]**

A difference between the force fields is:

- Gravitational forces are always attractive; **[1 mark]**
- Electric forces can be attractive or repulsive; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

An alpha particle and an aluminium nucleus are isolated in a vacuum, as shown in Fig. 1.1. Each nucleus may be considered to be a point mass with a point charge.

An aluminium nucleus contains 13 protons.

The alpha particle and the aluminium nucleus are separated by a distance of 2.0 nm.

Calculate the electric force between the alpha particle and the aluminium nucleus.
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the electric force between the alpha and aluminium nuclei:

List the known quantities

- Distance between nuclei, *r* = 2.0 nm = 2.0 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m
- Coulomb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup> (from the data page)
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C (from the data page)
- Charge on alpha particle, *Q*<sub>*1*</sub> = 2*e* = 2 × (1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) C
- Charge on aluminium nucleus, *Q*<sub>*2*</sub> = 13*e* = 13 × (1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) C

Use Coulomb's law to calculate the electric force:

- Coulomb's law:  $F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $F = \frac{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) \times 2 \times 13 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{-19} } )^{2}}{( 2.0 \times 10^{- 9} )^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Electric force:  $F$ = 1.5 × 10<sup>–9</sup> N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

An alpha particle and an aluminium nucleus are isolated in a vacuum, as shown in Fig. 1.1. Each nucleus may be considered to be a point mass with a point charge.

An aluminium nucleus contains 13 protons. The alpha particle and the aluminium nucleus are separated by a distance of 2.0 nm. Calculate the electric force between the alpha particle and the aluminium nucleus. Electric force: F = 1.5 × 10^–9 N

The aluminium nucleus contains 27 nucleons in total.

(i) Calculate the gravitational force between the two nuclei.

[2]

(ii) Suggest why gravitational effects do not need to be accounted for in electric field calculations involving nuclei.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Calculate the gravitational force between the alpha and aluminium nuclei:

List the known quantities

- Distance between nuclei, *r* = 2.0 nm = 2.0 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m
- Gravitational constant, $G$ = 6.67 × 10<sup>–11</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>–2</sup> (from the formula sheet)
- Atomic mass unit, u = 1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup> kg
- Mass of alpha particle, *m*<sub>*1*</sub> = 4u = 4 × (1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup>)
- Mass of aluminium nucleus, *m*<sub>*2*</sub> = 27u = 27 × (1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup>)

Use Newton's law of gravitation to calculate the gravitational force:

- Newton's law of gravitation:  $F=\frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $F = \frac{( 6.67 \times 10^{- 11} ) \times 4 \times 27 \times ( 1.66 \times 10^{- 27} )^{2}}{( 2.0 \times 10^{- 9} )^{2}}$
- Gravitational force:  $F$ = 5.0 × 10<sup>–45</sup> N **[1 mark]**

(ii) Gravitational effects do not need to be accounted for because:

- The gravitational force between two nuclei is negligible / much smaller compared to the electric force; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
Three fixed isolated point charges, $Q_{1}$ , $Q_{2}$  and $Q_{3}$ are located as shown in Fig. 1.1 below.

![7-4-s-q--q3a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](assets/007-7-4-s-q-q3a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**FIg. 1.1**

$Q_{1}$ has a charge of –30 µC, $Q_{2}$ has a charge of 50 µC and $Q_{3}$ has a charge of 70 µC. $Q_{3}$ is equidistant from charges $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$. The right is taken as the positive x direction.

Calculate the magnitude of the electric force on $Q_{3}$ from:

(i) $Q_{1}$

[2]

(ii) $Q_{2}$

[1]
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Charge, $Q_{1}$ = –30 µC = –30 × 10<sup>–6</sup> C
- Charge, $Q_{2}$ = 50 µC = 50 × 10<sup>–6</sup> C
- Charge, $Q_{3}$ = 70 µC = 70 × 10<sup>–6</sup> C
- Distance of $Q_{3}$ from centre of charges = 5m
- Distance between $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ = 10 m
- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>

(i) Calculate force from $Q_{1}$ , $F_{13}$:

Calculate separation from each charge, *r*:

![7-4-s-q--q3a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](assets/008-7-4-s-q-q3a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

- From Pythagoras’s theorem *r* = $\sqrt{5^{2}+5^{2}}=5\sqrt{2}$ m **[1 mark]**

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force, $F_{13}$:

- Since the question asks for the <u>magnitude</u> of the resultant force, the minus sign of the negative charge is not required
- Recall Coulomb's Law: $F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r^{2}}$
- $F_{13}$ =$\frac{Q_{1}Q_{3}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r^{2}}$ = $\frac{( 30 \times 10^{- 6} ) \times ( 70 \times 10^{- 6} )}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 8.85 \times 10^{- 12} ) \times ( 5 \sqrt{2} )^{2}}$
- $F_{13}$ = 0.3777 = 0.38 N **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate force from $Q_{2}$ , $F_{23}$:

- $F_{23}$ = $\frac{Q_{2} Q_{3} }{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} r^{2}} = \frac{( 50 \times 10^{- 6} ) \times ( 70 \times 10^{- 6} )}{4 \pi \times ( 8.85 \times 10^{- 12} ) \times ( 5 \sqrt{2} )^{2}}$
- $F_{23}$ = 0.6294 = 0.63 N **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Three fixed isolated point charges, Q1, Q2 and Q3 are located as shown in Fig. 1.1 below. Q1 has a charge of –30 µC, Q2 has a charge of 50 µC and Q3 has a charge of 70 µC. Q3 is equidistant from charges Q1 and Q2. The right is taken as the positive x direction.
Force from Q1, F13 = 0.3777 N. Force from Q2, F23 = 0.6294 N.
θ13 = 135º, θ23 = 45º (directions with respect to positive x-axis).

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force on $Q_{3}$.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Force from $Q_{1}$ , $F_{13}$= 0.3777 N (From part a)
- Force from $Q_{2}$, $F_{23}$ = 0.6294 N (From part a)

![7-4-s-q--q3c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](assets/011-7-4-s-q-q3c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Calculate the x and y components of the resultant force, $R$:

- $R_{x}$ = $F_{23x}$  ­–  $F_{13x}$= 0.6294 cos(45) – 0.3777 cos(45) = 0.17798 N **[1 mark]**
- $R_{y}$ = $F_{23y}$ + $F_{13y}$ = 0.6294 sin(45) + 0.3777 sin(45) = 0.71213 N **[1 mark]**

Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force *R* using vector addition:

- *R* =$\sqrt{( R_{x} )^{2} + ( R_{y} )^{2}}$ = $\sqrt{( 0.17798 )^{2} + ( 0.71213 )^{2}}$
- *R* = 0.734 N **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *This is also a case of Pythagoras' theorem where **F*<sub>*13*</sub>* and **F*<sub>*23*</sub>* are perpendicular to each other. The method shown works for all angles if you come across other similar questions. Remember that the x component of the resultant force is the net horizontal force from both *$Q_{1}$* and *$Q_{2}$*, and similarly for the y component. Don't forget it is standard convention to take the right hand side as positive and the left hand side as negative. *

![7-4-s-q--q3c-ma-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](assets/012-7-4-s-q-q3c-ma-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

parts.problem_md: State Coulomb’s law.
parts.solution_md:
Coulomb’s law states:

- The (electric) force between <u>two point charges</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Many definitions in A–level physics involve describing an equation in words. Remember that Coulomb’s law is equal to*

$F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$

> *Therefore, *$F\proptoQ_{1}Q_{2}$* (force is proportional to the product of the **two **charges) and *$F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$*  (force is inversely proportional to the square of their separation)*

parts.problem_md:
Two point charges of +3.2 × 10<sup>−15</sup> C and –3.2 × 10<sup>−15</sup> C are separated by a distance of 5.0 mm.

Calculate the magnitude of the electric force acting on each point charge.
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the magnitude of the electric force acting on each point charge:

List the known quantities:

- Magnitude of the charges, *q* = 3.2 × 10<sup>–15</sup> C
- Separation between the charges, *r* = 5.0 mm = 5.0 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- Coulomb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup> (from data page)

Use Coulomb’s law to calculate the force between the point charges:

- Coulomb’s law:  $F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $F = \frac{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) ( 3.2 \times 10^{-15} } )^{2}}{( 5.0 \times 10^{- 3} )^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Electric force:  $F$ = 3.7 × 10<sup>–15</sup> N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In this question, you are asked to calculate the **magnitude** of the electric force acting on each point charge. This means that you do **not** need to include the negative sign in your answer. A negative sign simply indicates that the electric force between the positive and negative point charges is **attractive**.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Two point charges of +3.2 × 10^−15^ C and –3.2 × 10^−15^ C are separated by a distance of 5.0 mm. Calculate the magnitude of the electric force acting on each point charge.

State and explain the effect on the magnitude of the electric force between the two point charges if, separately,

(i) the magnitude of one of the charges doubles

[2]

(ii) the separation between the charges increases.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) If the magnitude of one of the charges doubles, the electric force:

- Doubles; **[1 mark]**
- (Because) electric force is directly proportional to the magnitude of each point charge **OR** $F\proptoQ_{1}Q_{2}$; **[1 mark]**

(ii) If the separation between the charges increases, the electric force:

- Decreases; **[1 mark]**
- (Because) electric force and distance follow an inverse square law **OR** $F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
Helium-3 is a light, stable isotope of helium with two protons and one neutron.

The protons are assumed to be 1.88 × 10<sup>–15</sup> m apart.

For the two protons, calculate:

(i) the electrostatic force,

[2]

(ii) the gravitational force.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Separation of the proton, *r*  = 1.88 × 10<sup>–15</sup> m

(i) The electrostatic force is:

From the formulae page:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>** OR **$\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$** **= 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup>
- Elementary charge, *e  *= 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C

Calculate the electrostatic force, *F*<sub>E</sub>:

- $F_{E}=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $F_{E} = \frac{ ( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{-19} } ) \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} )}{( 1.88 \times 10^{- 15} )^{2}}$
- $F_{E}=65N$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) The gravitational force is:

From the formulae page:

- Rest mass of proton, *m*<sub>p</sub>  = 1.67 × 10<sup>–27</sup> kg
- Gravitational constant, *G*  = 6.67 × 10<sup>–11</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>–2</sup>

Calculate the gravitational force, *F*<sub>G</sub>:

- $F_{G}=\frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $F_{G} = \frac{( 6.67 \times 10^{- 11} ) \times ( 1.67 \times 10^{- 27} ) \times ( 1.67 \times 10^{- 27} ) }{( 1.88 \times 10^{- 15} )^{2}}$
- $F_{G}=5.263\times10^{-35}=5.3\times10^{-35}N$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Although it looks like the question hasn't given you many of the values needed, remember there are many given on the **data and formulae page** of your exam paper. The common ones to look out for are:*

- *Permittivity of free space, **ε*<sub>*0*</sub>
- *Rest mass of a proton, **m*<sub>*p*</sub>
- *Rest mass of an electron, **m*<sub>*e*</sub>
- *Elementary charge, **e** (this is the charge of an electron **and** proton - the only difference is the electron is negative whilst the proton is positive!)*

> *You don't need to remember any of these values. Using the formulae page during your revision will make it easier by the time it comes to your exam to find the values you want!*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Helium-3 is a light, stable isotope of helium with two protons and one neutron. The protons are assumed to be 1.88 × 10^–15^ m apart. For the two protons, calculate: (i) the electrostatic force, (ii) the gravitational force.

From the mark scheme: The electrostatic force F_E = 65 N. The gravitational force F_G = 5.263 × 10^–35 = 5.3 × 10^–35 N.

The force that holds the protons together in the nucleus is known as the strong nuclear force.

Suggest how your answers in (a) give evidence for the existence of the strong nuclear force.
parts.solution_md:
The answers in (a) give evidence for the existence of the strong nuclear force because:

- The force of <u>repulsion</u> is (much) greater than the force of <u>attraction</u>; **[1 mark]**
- There must be another force of attraction / the strong nuclear force; **[1 mark]**
- To hold the nucleus together; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You can see from the numbers in part (a), **F*<sub>*E*</sub>* = 65 N (the force of **repulsion **between the protons) whilst **F*<sub>*G *</sub>*= 5.3 × 10*<sup>*–35*</sup>* N ) (the force of **attraction** between the protons). It wouldn't be enough to just say **F*<sub>*E*</sub>* > **F*<sub>*G*</sub>*, you must relate your answer to attractive and repulsive forces. *

> *Without the strong nuclear force, we wouldn't have nuclei (and therefore wouldn't exist!) since the electrostatic repulsion between protons would mean they could never be close together. Since neutrons are neutral (no charge) there are no electrostatic forces between them.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Helium-3 is a light, stable isotope of helium with two protons and one neutron. The protons are assumed to be 1.88 × 10^–15^ m apart. For the two protons, calculate: (i) the electrostatic force, (ii) the gravitational force.

State why the radius of the protons is not taken into account when calculating the electrostatic force between them.
parts.solution_md:
The radius of the protons is not taken into account when calculating the electrostatic force between them because:

- They are assumed to be <u>point charges</u> /  <u>charged point masses</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Although they're most likely not, protons can be assumed to be spherical charges. Just like a spherical conductor, or a point outside a spherical conductor, the charge on the sphere may be considered to be a **point charge** at its centre. *

parts.problem_md:
The electrostatic force between an electron in the ground state of the helium-3 atom and the protons is 92 nN.

Show that the distance between the electron and the protons in the nucleus is about 50 pm.
parts.solution_md:
The distance between the electrons and the protons in the nucleus is:

List the known quantities:

- Electrostatic force, *F = *92 nN = 92 × 10<sup>–9</sup> N

From the formulae page:

- Permittivity of free space, = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>** OR **$\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$** **= 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup>
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19 </sup>C

Determine an equation for the distance, *r*:

- $F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- $r=\sqrt{\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}F}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- $r = \sqrt{ \frac{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{-19} } ) \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} )}{92 \times 10^{- 9} } }$ **[1 mark]**
- $r=50\times10^{-12}=50\mathrm{pm}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
Two point charges A and B are placed 0.014 mm apart as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![18-1-2b-m-charges-and-distance-for-coulombs-law-sq-cie-a-level](assets/016-18-1-2b-m-charges-and-distance-for-coulombs-law-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The charge of A is +3.1 nC and the charge of B is −6.2 nC. Determine the magnitude of the force between the two charges.
parts.solution_md:
Determine the magnitude of the force between the two charges:

List the known quantities:

- Charge A, *Q*<sub>*A*</sub> = +3.1 nC = 3.1 × 10<sup>−9</sup> C
- Charge B, *Q*<sub>*B*</sub> = −6.2 nC = −6.2 × 10<sup>−9</sup> C
- Distance between charges, *r* = 0.014 mm = 0.014 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m

- $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>−1</sup>

Use Coulomb's Law to calculate the force between the charges:

- $F=\frac{Q_{A}Q_{B}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- $F = ( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) \times \frac{( 3.1 \times 10^{-9} } ) \times ( 6.2 \times 10^{- 9} )}{( 0.014 \times 10^{- 3} )^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $F = 881.6 \mathrm{N} = 880 \mathrm{N} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The question is asking for the **magnitude **of the force, hence the **magnitude **of the charges only should be used in the calculation.*
